back: Growth whose benefits are widely shared across income groups and regions, with the poor taking part and gaining.
Growth that meets the needs of the present without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
The stock of natural resources and ecosystems (minerals, forests, soils, water, the atmosphere) that supplies inputs and services.

front: How can you tell whether growth was inclusive?
back: Compare the growth of the poorest groups with average growth, check income shares and whether the Gini coefficient rose or fell.

front: Why does GDP overstate sustainable growth?
back: It does not deduct the depletion of natural resources or the damage to the environment.

front: Name four policies for sustainable growth.
back: Carbon or pollution taxes, regulation, tradable permits and investment or subsidies for renewable energy.

front: Name policies that make growth more inclusive.
back: Education and health spending, rural infrastructure, support for small producers and progressive taxes with transfers.

front: Why is a carbon tax possibly regressive?
back: Poor households spend a larger share of income on energy, so the tax takes a larger share of their income.

front: Why is climate change a free-rider problem?
back: Each country gains from others' cuts in emissions while bearing the cost of its own, so it has an incentive not to act.
